catalog_quote: Perhaps the most vexing problem in Wes-kos is that of stress. The issue is clouded by the English stress and intonation patterns and the African languages which contribute their share with lexical tone problems. I have been able to find a short series of lexical items in Wes-kos which fit into the African lexical tone pattern. The African speakers -- not the English schooled West Cameroonian -- place stress on the last syllable of a word especially those which end in high vowels /i/ and /u/. Since lexical tone does not play a very big role in any of the English borrowings the issue carries no great trouble in unintelligibility. ... II. STRESSED INITIAL VOWELS. ... /ápsen/ < 'absent' ... /óda/ < 'other' ... /áfta/ < 'after'

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: The quotation was checked again. File, p. 125 = printed p. 53, header "FIRST STEPS in WES-KOS / UNIT FOUR PART FOUR / SOUNDS: STRESS AND TONE IN WES-KOS". Rendered the page scan (110 dpi) and read it: the whole passage from "Perhaps the most vexing problem in Wes-kos is that of stress." to "..the issue carries no great trouble in unintelligibility." is there word for word as quoted (the compiler "--" renders the typescript's double hyphen; the extracted text garbles "English schooled West Cameroonian" as "Englisn schooled /est Caneroonian" and "great" as "rroat", but the page scan is clean). Section II "STRESSED INITIAL VOWELS" lists /ápsen/ 'absent', /óda/ 'other', /áfta/ 'after' with acut…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Schneider (1963) treats Wes-kos/Cameroon Pidgin as mixed: a small set of lexical items carry African-style lexical tone, while stress is otherwise present but variable between speaker groups -- speakers without English schooling put stress on the final syllable of a word (especially words ending in /i/ or /u/), whereas English-schooled speakers keep English-like stress. Same page lists stressed initial vowels /ápsen/ 'absent', /óda/ 'other', /áfta/ 'after' (English stress retained). Later sources (Bellama et al. 1983 pp. iii-iv; Schröder 2013 APiCS §4; Yakpo 2021 p. 7) describe the language with two tones H/L and tonal minimal pairs (bábà 'barber' vs bàbá 'father', pópò 'proper' vs pòpó 'pawpaw'), and APiCS reports the tone-language question as unresolved (Menang 2008: 147). No modern opened source gives a word-stress placement rule.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: Speaker-group split: final-syllable stress is attributed to 'African speakers' but not to English-schooled West Cameroonians; stress placement also said to shift for expressive effect in reduplications (p. 7). Bellama 1983 p. vii: in diphthong spellings 'ia/ie' the accent is on the i, in 'ya/ye' on the second letter.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level ('last syllable of a word'), from a 1963 pedagogical course based on Kumba/West Cameroon speakers; no instrumental evidence. Tone statements in Bellama 1983 and APiCS are word-level minimal pairs.
new_statements.identity_note: Schneider 1963 calls the language 'Wes-kos' (West Coast English), his name for the Cameroon (Kumba/West Cameroon) variety of West African Pidgin English = came1254 (APiCS 18 'Cameroon Pidgin English', Glottolog came1254, autoglossonym Kamtok). Bellama 1983 and APiCS describe the same language. Note the speaker-group split in Schneider's statement (non-English-schooled vs English-schooled speakers).

tone_statements.citation: Steien, Guri Bordal & Kofi Yakpo. 2020. Romancing with tone: On the outcomes of prosodic contact. Language 96(1): 1-41. doi:10.1353/lan.2020.0000
tone_statements.quote: Other works cover aspects of the prosodic systems of ... Cameroon Pidgin English (Nkengasong 2016) ... The sources suggest that the prosodic systems of these languages show the characteristic outcomes of stress-to-tone mapping. They have two-tone systems in which most content words of English origin feature an obligatory and culminative H tone, while African-sourced content words show diverse tone patterns, including ones with no H tone at all. [p. 23]
tone_statements.check: quotation from a journal article located by the 2026-09-24 journal search, not yet verified by a second reading
tone_statements.summary: Second-hand (Nkengasong 2016): a two-tone system with one H on the English-stressed syllable of English-derived content words. Consistent with the catalog's tonal entry.

sources.note: p. 53: stress is 'the most vexing problem'; African (non-English-schooled) speakers place stress on the last syllable of a word, especially words ending in /i/ /u/; a short series of lexical items fit an African lexical-tone pattern; lexical tone plays little role in English borrowings. Gives stressed-initial-vowel examples /ápsen/ 'absent', /óda/ 'other', /áfta/ 'after' (p. 53); p. 36: object suffix /-am/ is not stressed; stressed schwa > /o/, unstressed > /a/ (p. 54).

sources.note: §4 Phonology: 'The question whether Cameroon Pidgin English is a tone language or not remains unresolved' (quoting Menang 2008: 147); most studies agree tone can be meaning-distinguishing, minimal pairs /bábà/ 'barber' vs /bàbá/ 'father', /pópò/ 'proper' vs /pòpó/ 'pawpaw'. Nothing about stress.

sources.citation: Yakpo, Kofi. 2021. Creole prosodic systems are areal, not simple. Frontiers in Psychology 12: 690593.
sources.note: Second-hand/survey: groups Cameroon Pidgin with the African English-lexifier creoles as 2-tone (/H, L/) systems; cites Nkengasong 2016: 36-37 for tone deletion/replacement in compounding and reduplication in Cameroon Pidgin; author's preliminary field data suggest the tone functions found in Pichi/Krio/Nigerian Pidgin 'are also found in Ghanaian Pidgin and Cameroon Pidgin' (p. 7). No stress placement rule.
